281.title: Home to the porch
281.hook: after seven visits, a deeper look at the school this path quotes most
281.carry: the fence, the soil, the fruit
281.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism today often keep a short line from Epictetus, Seneca or Marcus Aurelius close by and reread it in the morning or when something goes wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vaisakhi, the harvest and the founding of the Khalsa. Your line was a new beginning.

Seven weeks. Seven doors. You sat in a Hindu home with a lamp and a flower, took refuge with Buddhists, argued over a page with Jewish students, walked with Christians and with Catholics, fasted with Muslims, and ate on the floor with Sikhs. Each time you were a guest, and a good guest goes home. So where is home on this path? If you've walked it from the start, you know: the voice that argued with itself under the blankets, the enslaved teacher, the man who wrote letters about time. Home is the Stoa.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS, SEVEN DOORS.` → `A GOOD GUEST GOES HOME.` → `HOME TO THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: Back on day twenty-seven you met the porch itself: the Stoa Poikile, the painted colonnade on the edge of the market in Athens, where, Diogenes Laërtius tells us, a shipwrecked merchant named Zeno started teaching. The school was named after the porch. Since then this path has leaned on three writers of the Roman era more than anyone: Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. This month goes deeper, so it helps to know the shape of the whole school first. Stoics split philosophy into three parts: logic, how to think clearly; physics, how the world works; and ethics, how to live. Diogenes Laërtius, who collected their lives, reports that they liked to picture it as a fenced orchard. Logic is the fence. Physics is the soil and the trees. Ethics is the fruit. You can't have the fruit without the rest. Now the honest part. Almost everything the early Greek Stoics wrote is lost. Chrysippus, the school's great systematizer, is said to have written more than seven hundred books. Not one survives whole. What's left are fragments quoted by other people, often by critics. The Stoicism that reaches us whole is the late Roman version, practical and personal, written by men who were trying to live it. So the next weeks go in order: what the Stoics said is good, how they saw feelings, their picture of the world, and then the Stoics honestly, with their blind spots. First, where Epictetus starts his Handbook, in George Long's 1877 translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not."

282.title: Character is the good
282.hook: for the Stoics only virtue is truly good, and health and money are extras
282.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often weigh a decision by asking what a person of good character would do, putting that above what they stand to gain or lose.

segments.voice: Yesterday: home to the Stoa, and the whole school pictured as an orchard: the fence, the soil, the fruit.

Imagine a wish list for your life. Most of us could fill it in without thinking: good health, enough money, maybe more than enough, a decent job, people who like us, a nice place to live. Now a philosopher reads it over your shoulder and says: those are fine. Pleasant, even. But not one of them is actually good. Only one thing is good, and it's not on your list. The Stoics said exactly that, and they meant it. Their word for it: arete.
screen: `HEALTH, MONEY, A GOOD JOB.` → `FINE, BUT NOT GOOD.` → `ARETE.`

segments.voice: Arete is Greek, usually translated virtue, but the Greek word is wider and more practical. It means excellence, being good at what a thing is for. The arete of a knife is cutting well. The arete of a horse is running well. So what is a human being for? The Stoics answered: we're the animals that reason and live together. Our excellence is reasoning well and treating each other well. In a word, character. Then the bold claim: character is the only thing that's truly good, and bad character the only thing that's truly bad. Here's their test. A good thing should be good for you in every situation; it can never be used badly. Money fails: it can buy a meal for a hungry friend, or a bribe. Health fails: a strong body can help a neighbor move, or hurt someone. Even cleverness can be used for a con. But wisdom? Justice? Courage? The Stoics said these can't be turned to a bad use, because using things well is exactly what they are. Nobody does harm with too much justice. That's why Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, keeps coming back to one idea: the only good is what is honorable, and a person is measured by that and nothing else. The Stoics weren't against health or money. Tomorrow and the day after, you'll see they gladly preferred them. But they wouldn't stake a life on them. Lose your job and keep your honesty, and the Stoic says you've lost something pleasant and kept the thing that matters. It's a demanding idea. It's also strangely freeing.

283.title: Four virtues
283.howItsDone: Modern Stoic practitioners often pick one of the four virtues as a focus for the day and review in the evening where it showed up or went missing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arete, excellence, and the Stoic claim that character is the only true good. Your line was character first.

If character is the only good, what does it look like? Not in a sermon. On a Wednesday. When the kid spills the juice, when the boss asks you to fudge a number, when the last slice of cake is looking at you. The Stoics didn't leave it vague. They had a short list, four words long, inherited from Plato and turned into a daily tool. It would fit on a sticky note.
screen: `WHAT DOES CHARACTER LOOK LIKE?` → `ON A WEDNESDAY.` → `FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are. Wisdom: seeing clearly what's good, what's bad and what doesn't matter, and knowing what to do. Courage: doing the right thing when it's frightening or uncomfortable, and bearing what has to be borne. Justice: treating people fairly and kindly, doing your part for the common good. And self-control, sometimes called temperance or moderation: wanting things in the right measure, not being dragged around by appetite. The Greek word for that last one is sophrosyne, literally something like a sound mind, a safe and healthy way of thinking. Plato had already named these four. Much later, Christian writers took them up as the cardinal virtues, from the Latin for a hinge: the virtues a good life swings on. Now the Stoic twist. These aren't four separate skills you collect like badges. They're one excellence seen from four sides, and you can't really have one without the others. Courage without justice: a bold thief. Is that courage? The Stoics said no, that's just nerve. Justice without wisdom: meaning well and making a mess. Self-control without courage: a careful coward. Each virtue needs the others to be itself. Marcus Aurelius, writing to himself, says that if he ever finds anything in life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, he should turn to it with his whole soul. It reads as a dare to himself, and the four still stand. That makes the list practical. In any moment, four questions: what's true here, what's brave, what's fair, and what's enough?

284.title: Nice, not needed
284.hook: Stoics prefer health and wealth but don't stake their happiness on them
284.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners enjoy comforts and pursue sensible goals like health and income, while reminding themselves that these are preferred, not necessary for a good life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four virtues, wisdom, courage, justice and self-control. Your line was one excellence, four sides.

Two days ago the Stoics said health and money aren't truly good. Easy to say from a marble bench. So does a Stoic shrug at a broken leg? Turn down a raise? Live on cold water and gravel? No. The reason is a careful piece of sorting: the difference between something you'd like and something you need. A warm coat on a cold day. A good night's sleep. A full fridge. Nice. Very nice. The Stoic word for them is adiaphora.
screen: `SO A STOIC SHRUGS AT A BROKEN LEG?` → `NO.` → `ADIAPHORA.`

segments.voice: Adiaphora is Greek for indifferents, things that don't make a difference. Not to your comfort; there they make a big difference. They make no difference to whether you're a good person. Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself: all indifferent in that one sense. But the Stoics sorted the indifferents. Some are preferred: health over sickness, enough money over poverty, friends over loneliness. It's natural and sensible to pick those, and a Stoic will. Others are dispreferred, and it's sensible to avoid them. Zeno explained the word preferred with a picture from a royal court, which Cicero passes on. At court, the ministers and nobles are promoted, placed near the throne. But none of them is the king. Health and money are like that: high in rank, never the ruler. Only character sits on the throne. Seneca was a very rich man, and in his essay On the Happy Life he answers critics who threw that at him. Roughly: the wise person may own wealth, but wealth must not own him. Epictetus gives the gentlest picture of all, in his Handbook: behave in life as at a banquet. When a dish comes around to you, reach out and take a polite share. If it passes you by, don't grab at it. If it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch across the table. Enjoy what's in front of you. Just don't stake your happiness on the next plate.

285.title: Emotions as judgments
285.hook: Stoics saw destructive passions as mistaken judgments, not feeling itself
285.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners, and modern cognitive therapies influenced by them, look for the belief inside a strong emotion and ask whether it is accurate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adiaphora, the indifferents, preferred but not needed. Your line was take a polite share.

Your friend doesn't text back. An hour. Three hours. By evening you're sure: they're annoyed with you, maybe finished with you. Your stomach is tight. Then the phone buzzes. Sorry, phone died, what's up? The whole storm is gone in a second. Nothing changed in the world. Only the story you were telling yourself changed. The Stoics built a whole theory of emotion on moments like that one.
screen: `NO TEXT BACK.` → `THE STORM, THEN THE BUZZ.` → `ONLY THE STORY CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Pathos is Greek, from a verb meaning to suffer, to undergo, to have something happen to you. English keeps it in pathetic and sympathy, and usually translates the Stoic word as passion. For the Stoics, a pathos was a passion in a narrow sense: a feeling that runs away with you, that you undergo instead of choose. They named four families: distress, fear, craving, and a kind of giddy, overexcited pleasure. Here's the surprising claim. Chrysippus, an early Stoic teacher, taught that these passions are judgments. Not the cause of a judgment, not a side effect. Inside every runaway feeling is a belief: something terrible has happened, or something terrible is coming, or I must have that, or this is the best thing ever. And the Stoics said the belief is often false, or at least much too big. Epictetus says it plainly in his Handbook, in George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Chrysippus had a picture for it. When you walk, you can stop whenever you want. When you run downhill, your legs carry you past the point where you meant to stop. A passion is running downhill. What the Stoics did not say: that all feeling is a mistake, or that you should become a stone. On the last day of this week you'll meet the good feelings they kept. What they said is that the destructive ones carry a hidden sentence. Find the sentence and you can check it. So the question that matters: what am I telling myself?

286.title: The first jolt
286.hook: Seneca: a jolt of shock isn't anger yet, agreeing with it is (On Anger 2.3)
286.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners treat a sudden flash of fear or anger as an involuntary first movement and pause before deciding whether to agree with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pathos, the runaway passion with a judgment hidden inside. Your line was what am I telling myself.

A ship in a storm, somewhere between Greece and Italy. The Roman writer Aulus Gellius is on board, and so is a famous Stoic philosopher. The waves get huge, and the philosopher goes white as a sheet. When the storm passes, a rich passenger mocks him: some Stoic, you were as scared as the rest of us. The philosopher brushes him off with a sharp reply. But when Gellius asks him, in earnest, why he went pale, he reaches into his bag, takes out a book of Epictetus, and shows him a passage. It's about primus motus.
screen: `A SHIP IN A STORM.` → `THE STOIC GOES WHITE.` → `SOME STOIC.`

segments.voice: Here's what the passage said, as Gellius retells it. When something frightening appears, even the mind of a wise person is shaken for a moment. It flinches, goes pale, jumps. That's not a failure; it's how a body works. What the wise person doesn't do is agree with it, go on to think: yes, this is truly terrible. The fool agrees, and adds more. Seneca laid out the same idea in his essay On Anger. He lists things nobody chooses: a shiver when cold water splashes you, dizziness at the edge of a cliff, a blush, the hair standing up on your arms at bad news. He calls these first movements. They happen to us. They are not yet anger, or fear. Anger, Seneca says, comes in a second step, when the mind signs off on the jolt: I've been wronged, and they should pay. A third step follows, when it's out of control and no longer cares whether it's right. Three moments: the jolt, the yes, the runaway. The jolt isn't yours to stop. The yes is. That's a relief. A flash of anger in traffic, a stab of jealousy at a friend's good news, a lurch of panic at an email, isn't proof you're a bad person or a failed Stoic. It's weather passing through a body, and you're the one who decides whether to agree with it. As yesterday taught, agreeing is where the story starts. Gellius says he found the answer satisfying. The philosopher had been pale. He hadn't said yes.

287.title: Good feelings
287.hook: the Stoics kept joy, wise wishing and caution
287.howItsDone: Modern Stoic practitioners distinguish calm joy from excited pleasure and caution from fear, and try to cultivate the steady versions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: primus motus, the flinch that comes before anger or fear. Your line was the jolt isn't me.

After a week on the porch, you might picture the Stoic with the joy dialed down to zero. Character is the only good. Comforts are just preferred. Feelings have judgments hiding in them. Check the jolt before you agree. It can sound like a person who never laughs at a wedding. But the Stoics had a word for the feelings they wanted more of. Not fewer feelings. Better ones.
screen: `JOY DIALED DOWN TO ZERO?` → `NOT FEWER FEELINGS.` → `BETTER ONES.`

segments.voice: Eupatheia is Greek: eu, good or well, plus pathos, the word we met two days ago. Good feelings. Diogenes Laërtius reports that the Stoics named three, each the healthy twin of a passion. Instead of giddy, grasping pleasure, joy: a calm, deep gladness at what's truly good. Instead of craving, wishing: wanting something wisely, in the right measure. Instead of fear, caution: sensible care about real dangers, like looking both ways without panicking about the traffic. The same report lists finer kinds under each: under wishing, goodwill and warm affection; under joy, delight and cheerfulness. Notice: three twins for four passions. There's no good version of distress for the fully wise person, because the Stoics thought such a person had nothing truly bad to grieve over. That's one of their hardest claims, and i'll be honest about it in two weeks. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, says, roughly, believe me, real joy is a serious thing. Not a sugar rush: steady, from inside, and it doesn't vanish when the party ends. So look back at this week. Home to the porch. Arete, character first. The four virtues. Adiaphora, nice not needed. Pathos, and the sentence inside a feeling. Primus motus. And now the good feelings. The goal was never a cold life. It was a clear one, with room for gladness no one can take.
screen: `EU + PATHOS: GOOD FEELINGS.` · `JOY, WISHING, CAUTION.` · `REAL JOY IS A SERIOUS THING.` · `THE WEEK ON THE PORCH.` · then, large: `JOY IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Find one good feeling that's here right now, or was here today: gladness at the light, relief, warmth for someone, the quiet satisfaction of a task done. Let it be exactly as big as it is, not inflated, not waved away. Rest in it, breathing.
Eupatheia. Greek for good feelings: joy, wise wishing and caution, the healthy twins of the passions.
